messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Plumber
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 69

She came in clutching a worn leather tool belt, the kind with pouches for wrenches and pipe cutters. She set it on the floor beside the chair and smoothed the knees of her coveralls, stained with copper dust and joint compound. For the first few minutes she stared at a loose thread on her sleeve, pulling it until it snapped. Then she began.

It started three years ago. She had gone to the hospital for what was supposed to be a routine gallbladder removal. A laparoscopic procedure, in and out. But a small tear in her bile duct went unnoticed. Within days she was back in the emergency room with a fever so high she could not tell the ceiling from the floor. Sepsis. The doctors told her family she might not make it.

She remembers the ICU in fragments: the rhythmic hiss of the ventilator, the cold pressure of a central line being threaded into her neck, the face of a nurse who kept saying her name in a calm, steady voice. She remembers the terror of not being able to move, of feeling her body sink into the mattress like lead into a drain. For eleven days she hovered between waking and dreaming, and when she finally opened her eyes, she did not recognize her own hands—thin, pale, covered in tape.

The physical recovery took months. She lost muscle, lost weight, lost the calluses on her palms that had come from thirty years of wrenching pipes under sinks and boiling water heaters. Her family—her mother, her two older sisters—hovered, brought her bowls of warm dal and rice, urged her to rest. They also started asking when she would “settle down,” marry, have children. She was forty-two at the time, the youngest daughter, the one who had always worked with her hands instead of following the traditional path. The illness made their questions more urgent, as if her near-death had exposed a final window of opportunity.

She went back to work too soon. The first job was a clogged toilet in a basement apartment. The moment she stepped into the small, windowless bathroom, the smell of bleach and stale water hit her, and she felt her chest tighten. The room felt like the ICU—small, enclosed, with no way out. Her hands shook so badly she could not fit the snake into the pipe. She sat on the floor, breathing in shallow gasps, until the homeowner asked if she was okay.

Now she avoids certain calls. No more jobs in hospital basements or nursing homes. She will not work in any room with a locked door, not even if it is a customer’s bathroom with a child’s lock on the inside. She carries a small battery-powered fan in her truck, because the sound of a ventilation unit reminds her of the ventilator. When she drives past the hospital where she was treated, she takes the long way around, even if it adds twenty minutes.

At night she wakes drenched in sweat, convinced the fever is back. She feels her forehead, checks her temperature with a digital thermometer she keeps on her nightstand. Sometimes she cannot tell if the cold she feels is real or remembered. She has stopped going to family gatherings because her mother’s kitchen smells like the dal she was fed in recovery. She has stopped answering calls from her sisters, who still ask about marriage.

She tells me she is fine. She works. She pays her bills. But her PCL-5 score is 69, and she carries the tool belt everywhere, even to her weekly appointments, as if it is the only part of her the illness could not take.
